entries.meaning: In the palace were varied garments, pillows and couches, soft, spotless, and lovely as milk foam. There Sītā and Rāma used to sleep at night, their own beauty humbling even Rati and Love. Now that same Sītā and Rāma lay upon a bed of grass, weary and wearing only simple cloth, scarcely recognizable. Mother, father, kindred, townspeople, virtuous friends, servants, and maids had guarded them like their own lives, yet that very lord Rāma slept upon the ground. Sītā's father was Janaka, renowned throughout the world; her father-in-law was Raghu's king, friend of the lord of gods; her husband was Rāmacandra—and still Vaidehī slept on earth. To whom has Fate not been hostile? Were Sītā and Raghu's hero fit for forest life? People rightly say deeds are supreme. Guha blamed the dull-minded daughter of Kekaya, whose cruel crookedness had turned a season of joy into suffering for Raghunandana and Jānakī.

The misguided woman had become an axe against the tree of the solar dynasty and had made the whole world miserable. Seeing Rāma and Sītā sleep on the earth, the Niṣāda's grief became intense. Lakṣmaṇa then spoke sweet and gentle words steeped in knowledge, detachment, and devotion: no one gives another happiness or grief; each person experiences the fruit of his own deeds, brother. Union and separation, good and bad enjoyments, friend, foe and neutral party, the snares of delusion, birth and death, the whole worldly web, prosperity and adversity, action and time, earth, house, wealth, city, family, heaven and hell—everything grasped in worldly dealings, whether seen, heard, or pondered in the mind, is rooted in delusion and lacks ultimate reality. A pauper may become a king in a dream or the lord of heaven a beggar; upon waking neither gain nor loss remains. See the world's display in just this way.

Reflecting thus, Lakṣmaṇa said, do not become angry or blame anyone in vain. In the night of delusion everyone sleeps and sees dreams of many kinds. Yogins alone remain awake in this worldly night: seekers of the highest truth who have separated themselves from the display. Know that a living being has begun to awaken precisely when detachment from sensual pleasure repeatedly arises. When discernment appears and the bewilderment of delusion departs, love for Raghunātha's feet follows. Friend, this is the highest spiritual good: love for Rāma's feet in thought, deed, and speech. Rāma is Brahman, the form of highest reality—unmoving, unseen, beginningless, unequaled, free from every alteration and distinction, whom the Vedas continually describe by saying not this, not this. For the good of devotees, the earth, brahmins, cows, and gods, the compassionate one assumes a human body and enacts deeds whose hearing severs the world's net.

Understand this, friend, abandon delusion, and become devoted to the feet of Sītā and Raghu's hero. As Lakṣmaṇa spoke Rāma's virtues, dawn appeared and the source of the world's auspicious joy awoke. After completing all morning observances, Rāma bathed and, pure and wise, asked for the banyan's milk. He and his younger brother formed their hair into matted locks. Seeing this, tears clouded Sumantra's eyes; his heart burned, his face grew pale, and with hands joined he spoke in utter humility. King Daśaratha, lord of Kosala, had told him to take the chariot with Rāma, show him the forest, bathe him in the Gaṅgā, and quickly bring both brothers back; he must also return Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Sītā, dispelling every doubt and hesitation. The minister would do just as the king had commanded. Then, weeping like a child, he fell at Rāma's feet and pleaded.

Sumantra begged Rāma to show the mercy that would keep Ayodhyā from being orphaned. Rāma raised and instructed him: dear one, you have thoroughly examined every judgment of dharma. Kings Śibi, Dadhīci, and Hariścandra endured millions of afflictions for dharma; wise Rantideva and Bali also upheld it through many hardships. Scripture, Veda, and Purāṇa declare that no dharma equals truth. Rāma had obtained the chance to follow that duty with ease; if he abandoned it, infamy would cover the three worlds. For an honorable person, the gain of disgrace is a fierce burning equal to millions of deaths. What more could he tell Sumantra? If the minister answered his father on Rāma's behalf, Rāma himself would incur sin. He should clasp the king's feet, bow countless times, plead with joined hands, and ask him not to worry about Rāma in any matter.

Rāma continued: you are as dear and beneficial to me as a father. I join my hands and ask that you do everything necessary so my father suffers no pain through worry for me. Hearing the exchange between Raghunātha and the minister, Guha and all his kin became distraught. Lakṣmaṇa then uttered some bitter words, but his lord stopped him, judging them highly improper. Rāma made Sumantra swear by him and told him not to repeat Lakṣmaṇa's message. Sumantra then conveyed another message from the king: Sītā would not endure the forest's hardships, so Sumantra must use whatever means could bring her back to Ayodhyā. Otherwise, stripped of his very last support, the king would not live, like a fish without water. Sītā might live happily either with her parents or her in-laws, wherever her heart preferred, until the adversity passed.

The king's anguished and loving plea had been made in a manner beyond description. Hearing her father's message, the treasury of compassion taught Sītā in countless ways: by returning, she would remove the burden from parents-in-law, teacher, beloved family, and everyone else. Vaidehī answered her husband's words: listen, most loving lord of my life. You are supremely compassionate and discerning; how can a shadow remain after leaving the body? Where can radiance go after abandoning the sun, or moonlight after leaving the moon? After humbly addressing her love-filled husband, she spoke graceful words to Sumantra. He was her father-in-law's equal and her benefactor, so it was deeply improper for her to answer him back; yet grief had brought her before him, and she begged him not to consider it disrespect. Apart from the lotus feet of Ārya's son, every relationship wherever it extended was in vain.

Sītā said she had seen her father's splendor and pleasures: kings whose crowned heads touched the footstool before that jewel among monarchs. Yet without her beloved even such a joy-filled paternal home did not please her. Her father-in-law, lord of Kosala and sovereign emperor, had a glory manifest throughout the fourteen worlds; even Indra came before him and offered half his throne. Such was her father-in-law, Ayodhyā her home, and a dear family and mother-in-law hers—but without the pollen of Rāma's lotus feet no one gave her happiness even in a dream. The inaccessible road, forest ground, mountains, fierce lions, boundless lakes and rivers, Kol and Kirāta people, deer, and birds would all delight her in the company of the lord of her life. Sumantra should fall at her parents-in-law's feet and convey her plea: they must not worry about her at all, for by nature she would be happy in the forest.

The lord of her life and her dear brother-in-law were with her; Lakṣmaṇa, foremost among heroes, carried bow and quiver. Her mind would feel no toil, confusion, or pain on the road, and no one should worry about her even for a moment. Hearing Sītā's cooling words, Sumantra was distraught like a serpent that had lost its jewel. His eyes could not see, his ears could not hear, and in his agitation he could say nothing. Rāma consoled him in many ways, yet the burning in his breast did not cool. Sumantra made repeated efforts for their welfare, and Rāma answered each appropriately. Rāma's command could not be set aside, and the hard course of action lay beyond anyone's control. Bowing his head at Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā's feet, the minister turned back like a merchant who had lost his capital. As he drove, the horses looked repeatedly toward Rāma and neighed; seeing them, the Niṣādas beat their heads in grief.

If even animals were so distraught at separation from Rāma, how would his subjects, mother, and father live? Rāma compelled Sumantra to depart, then came to the bank of the celestial river. He asked for a boat, but the ferryman would not bring it. The boatman said he knew Rāma's secret: everyone says the dust of his lotus feet contains something that turns things into human beings. At its touch a stone had become a lovely woman; wood was no harder than stone. If the sage's wife emerged from his little ferry, the boat would be lost and block his livelihood, for with it he maintained his whole family and knew no other trade. If Rāma absolutely wished to cross, he must first allow the boatman to wash his lotus feet.
